views.label: Health
notes: Statuses are rules of thumb, not verdicts; each metric and diagnostic says which rule it uses. Each window includes this tool's own second sample: about 3 statements, with the temporary table and scans they need, and its connection.

views.label: Waits
notes: Some wait classes are not instrumented (mutexes 0 of 236 on, read/write locks 0 of 33 on, shared/exclusive locks 0 of 15 on, priority read/write locks 0 of 2 on, condition waits 0 of 56 on, socket i/o 0 of 7 on), so their waits are not in this report. No mutex or rwlock waits here never means no contention.
1 event(s) were counted but not timed, so they are not ranked: wait/io/socket/sql/client_connection.

Wait time is summed across all threads, background threads included, so it can exceed the wall-clock window. Table I/O includes the file I/O and internal lock waits inside each call, which are counted again under their own events, so the classes are never added up.
InnoDB asynchronous I/O (read-ahead, page cleaner writes) is timed only for submitting the request, so its latency is understated. Bytes are exact (see I/O).
Since server start covers 2 d 5 h of uptime; the longest single wait (max) is since start too, never per window.

views.label: I/O
notes: Table figures are row operations through the storage engine (rows fetched, inserted, updated, deleted) and their time, which includes the file I/O inside each call. They are not bytes; the files show bytes.
Temporary and deleted files leave the per-file list when closed; their I/O stays in the file kinds, so check those for sort and temporary table spills.
InnoDB asynchronous I/O (read-ahead, page cleaner writes) is timed only for submitting the request: bytes are right, latency is understated.
Since server start covers 2 d 5 h of uptime.

views.label: Parameters
notes: Counters run from server start. The connection peak (Max_used_connections) also restarts with FLUSH STATUS on MySQL and MariaDB 11.4 or older, and with FLUSH GLOBAL STATUS on MariaDB 11.5 and later, which also resets the temporary-table and tables-opened counts.
Statuses are rules of thumb, not verdicts; each check says which rule it uses. myflames never changes a setting: run a suggested statement only after reading its caveat.

views.label: InnoDB
notes: Each read of SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS restarts InnoDB's per-second averages for every reader. Statuses are rules of thumb from one snapshot, not verdicts; values that stay high across refreshes matter more than one reading.

views.label: Sessions
notes: Statuses are rules of thumb, not verdicts. The summary counts every session this account can see; the filters narrow only the list. This tool's own session is left out.

views.label: Instruments
notes: MySQL 8.4 and 9.x share these defaults in source, and MySQL 26.7 matched them on a live server; newer versions add instruments, not new defaults.

views.label: Server checks
notes: MySQL 8.0 and later have no query cache, so there is nothing to check for it.

views.label: Tables
notes: Row counts, sizes and free space come from a cache MySQL keeps for up to 1 d 0 h (information_schema_stats_expiry; partitioned tables are never cached), so they can be that old. Fresh numbers (--fresh) reads them from InnoDB now, for myflames' own connection only.

TABLE_ROWS, DATA_LENGTH and INDEX_LENGTH are InnoDB estimates from its table statistics, recalculated in the background after about 10% of the rows change (persistent statistics, the default) or by ANALYZE TABLE. DATA_FREE is read with the other statistics, so it comes from the same cache unless Fresh numbers is on. It counts whole free extents and the unused space at the end of the file (an extent is 1 MiB with 4 to 16 KiB pages, 2 MiB with 32 KiB, 4 MiB with 64 KiB), minus a reserve of 2 extents plus about 1%; free pages in partly used extents and half-empty pages after scattered deletes are not in it, so it understates.
Read every schema except mysql, sys, performance_schema and information_schema.

views.label: Indexes
notes: Unused means no row read, written or looked up through the index since the server started (2 d 5 h ago), or since an index on that table was added, dropped or renamed, or the table was renamed or rebuilt by copying, any of which restarts its counts. An index used only by a weekly or monthly job looks unused until the job runs.

Tables with no row read or written since the counts started (never opened, or opened only to read their definition) are listed under No data, never as unused. A TRUNCATE of a Performance Schema summary table also resets the counts.
The server has been up only 2 d 5 h, so infrequent jobs may not have run yet.

PRIMARY and UNIQUE indexes are never listed as unused: they enforce constraints even when no query reads them. Indexes that back a foreign key are marked keep: InnoDB checks foreign keys without going through the usage counters.
Counts are per server: reads on replicas are not included.

findings.title: Buffer pool size
findings.headline: 128.0 MiB
findings.verdict: innodb_buffer_pool_size (128.0 MiB) is much smaller than the InnoDB tablespace files (1.2 GiB).
findings.why: The memory InnoDB uses to cache data and index pages. Pages not in it are read from disk. Compared here with the size of the InnoDB tablespace files on disk (free space inside them included), because a pool much smaller than the data cannot hold much of it.
findings.rule: watch when the buffer pool is less than half the InnoDB tablespace files; a pool smaller than the data is normal when the hot data fits, so check the hit ratio in Health
findings.caveat: The data on disk includes cold rows and free space; what matters is the hot set. Leave room for connections, the OS and other processes: a pool that makes the server swap is far worse than disk reads.

action.text: Raise it within the memory the server can spare, if Health shows disk reads and a falling hit ratio. It can be resized online.

findings.title: Redundant indexes
findings.headline: 3 indexes
findings.verdict: 3 indexes are duplicates or leftmost prefixes of other indexes on their tables.
findings.why: idx_user (user_id) is a leftmost prefix of idx_user_status (user_id, status), so idx_user_status serves every lookup idx_user serves. Each extra index slows writes and uses buffer pool memory.
findings.rule: watch when an index is a duplicate or a leftmost prefix of another index on the same table
findings.caveat: Check for FORCE INDEX or USE INDEX hints that name it. Make it invisible first and run a full business cycle (month-end jobs, reports, replicas) before dropping it: an invisible index is still maintained on writes, but the optimizer stops using it, and making it visible again is instant. Queries with an index hint that names it fail while it is invisible.

action.text: Make it invisible first, then drop it.

findings.title: Binary log expiry
findings.headline: 30 d 0 h
findings.verdict: Binary logs expire after 30 d 0 h.
findings.why: Binary logs are kept until they expire or someone purges them; expiry runs at startup and when the server rotates to a new binary log.
findings.rule: watch when the binary log is on and nothing purges it automatically (no expiry period and no total size limit)

findings.title: Redo flush at commit
findings.verdict: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1.
findings.why: When InnoDB writes and syncs the redo log for a commit. 1 writes and syncs at every commit, so a committed transaction survives a crash or power loss.
findings.rule: ok at 1 (and MariaDB's 3), which make each commit durable; watch at 0 or 2

findings.title: Redo log size
findings.headline: 100.0 MiB
findings.verdict: Redo capacity 100.0 MiB; about 0 B/s of redo on average since startup, so it holds about 1714 d 11 h at that rate; the checkpoint age is 0 B now (0% of capacity; MySQL starts forced flushing near 79% and makes writes wait near 84%).
findings.why: The redo log holds changes not yet written to the data files. When it fills, InnoDB must flush dirty pages before more writes can proceed, so a small redo log for the write rate causes flushing bursts. A larger one means a longer crash recovery. MySQL's Innodb_os_log_written re-counts rewrites of partly filled blocks, so the rate is a little high.
findings.rule: watch when the redo capacity holds less than 1 hour of redo at the average rate since startup (judged after 60 minutes of uptime; peaks are higher than the average)
findings.caveat: Peaks write faster than the average, and a larger redo log makes crash recovery longer and uses more disk.

findings.title: Binary log sync
findings.verdict: sync_binlog=1.
findings.why: How often the binary log is synced to disk. At 1 it is synced at each commit (group), so after an OS crash or power loss the binary log has every committed transaction and replicas stay consistent. MySQL's default is 1.
findings.rule: ok at 1 with the binary log on; watch at 0 or above 1

findings.title: Binary log cache
findings.headline: No binary log writes
findings.verdict: No transaction wrote to the binary log in the window.
findings.why: With the binary log on, each session collects a transaction's events in memory (binlog_cache_size; binlog_stmt_cache_size for changes to non-transactional tables) and writes them to the binary log at commit. Events that do not fit spill to a temporary file on disk (Binlog_cache_disk_use, Binlog_stmt_cache_disk_use). The cache is per session, so a larger size is multiplied by the sessions that write.
findings.rule: watch when 10% or more of the transactions or statements that used a binary log cache spilled to a temporary file, with at least 5 spills in the window; never a problem

numbers.label: Non-transactional statements that spilled to disk

findings.title: Redo log size for the write rate
findings.headline: No redo in this window
findings.verdict: InnoDB wrote no redo in the window. The checkpoint age is 0 B (0% of the capacity).
findings.why: InnoDB writes every change to the redo log first. A checkpoint frees redo space once the matching dirty pages are flushed, so the capacity limits how far flushing can fall behind. The checkpoint age (Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn minus Innodb_redo_log_checkpoint_lsn) is how much of the capacity is in use. MySQL's redo-driven adaptive flushing starts early (about 8% of the capacity, innodb_adaptive_flushing_lwm) and grows with the age, reaches its age limit at about 73%, forces flushing from about 79% (innodb_flush_sync, on by default), and makes user writes wait from about 84%. These points compare the age of the oldest dirty page, which is at most the checkpoint age. A larger redo log smooths that out but makes crash recovery longer. Two counters measure redo. The log sequence number (Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn) grows by the redo generated, counted in 512-byte log blocks including their headers and trailers; it is what fills the capacity, so the times are computed from it. Innodb_os_log_written counts the bytes written to the redo files: the log writer rewrites the last, partly filled block on each write, so with many small commits it runs well above the redo generated. Innodb_log_waits counts waits for space in the in-memory log buffer (innodb_log_buffer_size), a different limit.
findings.rule: watch when the checkpoint age reaches about 73% of the capacity (where adaptive flushing reaches its age limit) in either sample, problem at about 79% (forced flushing); also watch when the capacity holds less than about 1 hour of redo at this window's rate (a common rule of thumb; this window may not be the peak) or when Innodb_log_waits grew

findings.title: Buffer pool: full or warming
findings.headline: 0 B/s read from disk
findings.verdict: The buffer pool is full (908 free pages, at or below the page cleaner's target of 1,024) and InnoDB read almost nothing from disk: 0 pages per second (0 B/s). The data this workload uses fits in memory.
findings.why: InnoDB keeps a small free list: while the server is busy, its page cleaner evicts the least recently used pages until each buffer pool instance has innodb_lru_scan_depth free pages, and an idle full pool can show 0 free pages (1,024 x 1 = 1,024 pages here). So "full" means free pages at or below that target, not zero. Once it is full, every page read from disk evicts another one. Bytes read from disk are the pages read from disk times innodb_page_size (16.0 KiB); MySQL adds Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead, because Innodb_buffer_pool_reads leaves out linear read-ahead. Innodb_data_read counts the bytes InnoDB read from its data files: it is lower for ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED tables, which read the smaller compressed page, and on MySQL it also counts redo log reads, but only during startup.
findings.rule: full when free pages are at or below innodb_lru_scan_depth x buffer pool instances (the free list InnoDB's page cleaner keeps). Full: ok below 10 pages read from disk per second, watch at 10 or more, problem when the hit ratio is also below 95%. Not full: no threshold

findings.verdict: 0 merge passes in the window for 0 sorts. Sorts fit in sort_buffer_size.
findings.why: A sort that cannot use an index (filesort) collects rows in sort_buffer_size. When they do not fit, it writes sorted runs to a temporary file and merges them, and each merge pass is counted in Sort_merge_passes. Sort_range and Sort_scan count the sorts themselves. sort_buffer_size is a limit for each sort in every session, so raise it for the sessions that need it rather than globally.

findings.verdict: At least 58 file descriptors are in use: 2 through the server's file layer, 55 InnoDB files and 1 connection, 0.0% of open_files_limit 1,048,576.
findings.why: open_files_limit is the most file descriptors the server process can hold. Open_files counts files the server opened through its own file layer (MyISAM and Aria tables, binary and relay logs, some temporary files), not InnoDB's, which Innodb_num_open_files counts; each client connection also uses a socket. myflames adds the three, a lower bound: other descriptors are not visible through SQL.
findings.rule: watch when the file descriptors myflames can account for reach 75% of open_files_limit, problem at 90%

findings.title: Table open cache
findings.headline: No misses
findings.verdict: No overflows in the window: the tables in use fit in the cache. 0.0% of 11 lookups missed. 790 of 4,000 cached instances are open.
findings.why: Each statement needs an open instance of every table it uses. A hit reuses a free instance from the cache. A miss opens a new one (Opened_tables): the first use of a table, or another session needing its own instance of a busy table, so misses alone are normal. An overflow means the cache was full and an unused instance was closed to make room: tables are being opened and closed over and over. MySQL divides table_open_cache across table_open_cache_instances.
findings.rule: watch at 1 overflow per second, problem at 10, with at least 5 in the window. Misses without overflows are not judged

findings.title: Table definition cache
findings.headline: 0 opened per second
findings.verdict: 0 table definitions were opened in the window (0 per second); 92 of 2,000 are cached.
findings.why: The definition cache keeps parsed table definitions (shares), separate from the open table instances. A definition is opened the first time a table is used, or again after it was evicted because the cache was full. Steady openings while the cache is full mean table_definition_cache is smaller than the number of tables in use.
findings.rule: watch when table definitions are opened at 1 per second or more (at least 5 in the window) while the definition cache is at least 95% full

findings.title: Table cache
findings.verdict: 790 of 4,000 in use; 0 tables opened per second on average since startup.
findings.why: How many open table instances the server keeps for reuse. When it is full, a table not in it must be opened again (Opened_tables).
findings.rule: watch when the cache is at least 95% full and tables were opened at 1 per second or more on average since startup
findings.caveat: Each open table uses a file descriptor and memory; the server needs open_files_limit to cover it. MySQL may lower table_open_cache at startup to fit open_files_limit.

findings.title: Free space inside tablespaces
findings.headline: none
findings.verdict: No file-per-table tablespace has free space at the rule's level.
findings.why: DATA_FREE against DATA_LENGTH + INDEX_LENGTH, judged only for file-per-table tablespaces.
findings.rule: watch when free space is at least 10% of the tablespace file and at least 100.0 MiB; problem at 25% and 1.0 GiB

findings.title: Tables without a usable key
findings.headline: 0 tables
findings.verdict: None in every user schema.
findings.why: InnoDB keeps each table as a B-tree ordered by the primary key, and every secondary index stores the primary key to reach the row. Without a primary key it uses the first unique key on NOT NULL columns (whole columns, not a prefix, a functional part or a virtual generated column). Without one it adds a hidden 6-byte row ID. With row-based replication (the default) each UPDATE or DELETE reaches the replica as the changed rows, and the replica has to find each one. With a primary key or a unique key on NOT NULL columns that is one index lookup per row. Without one, MySQL hashes the rows of each event and looks them up through another index if there is one, or else makes up to one full table scan per event. An event holds about 8 KiB of rows (binlog_row_event_max_size), so a large DELETE means many full scans and the replica falls behind.
findings.rule: problem: no PRIMARY KEY and no UNIQUE key on NOT NULL columns

findings.title: Tables clustered on a unique key, not a primary key
findings.headline: 0 tables
findings.verdict: None in every user schema.
findings.why: InnoDB keeps each table as a B-tree ordered by the primary key, and every secondary index stores the primary key to reach the row. Without a primary key it uses the first unique key on NOT NULL columns (whole columns, not a prefix, a functional part or a virtual generated column). Without one it adds a hidden 6-byte row ID. With row-based replication (the default) each UPDATE or DELETE reaches the replica as the changed rows, and the replica has to find each one. With a primary key or a unique key on NOT NULL columns that is one index lookup per row. Without one, MySQL hashes the rows of each event and looks them up through another index if there is one, or else makes up to one full table scan per event. An event holds about 8 KiB of rows (binlog_row_event_max_size), so a large DELETE means many full scans and the replica falls behind.
findings.rule: watch: no PRIMARY KEY, but a UNIQUE key on NOT NULL columns stands in for it

attribution.label: text match, not proof
caveats: The table is matched by name in the normalized digest text, so this is a text match, not proof: a view, a stored routine or a trigger can read the table without naming it, an alias or another schema's table with the same name can match, and digest text is cut at performance_schema_max_digest_length (1024 bytes by default).
SUM_NO_INDEX_USED and SUM_SELECT_SCAN count per statement, not per table: a statement that names this table can match because it scanned another table it reads.
SCHEMA_NAME is the session's default schema, not the table's: an unqualified name matches only digests whose default schema is the table's schema.
notes: Counters accumulate since the server started or the digest table was last truncated.

Listed: statements that read a later table of a join with a full scan (SUM_SELECT_FULL_JOIN, the per-statement form of Select_full_join; on MariaDB a full table scan only) or with a range check for each row (SUM_SELECT_RANGE_CHECK). Health counts the same events over its window; these sums run since the digest was first seen.
